D
iminishing inappropriate neovascularization has great promise as a therapeutic approach.  Support for
this approach was recently provided by the market introduction of two anti-angiogenic drugs, Avastin and
Macugen to treat colon cancer and Age Related Macular Degeneration, respectively. In particular, the use
of  anti-angiogenic  inhibitors  to  treat  cancer  is  widely  anticipated  because  the  concept  is  so  simple  and
attractive:  Inhibit  the  growth  of  genetically  stable  endothelial  cells,  and  most  tumors  should  starve  to
death because of the lack of oxygen and nutrients or partially inhibit endothelial growth and prune chaotic
tumor vasculature to make chemotherapy and/or radiation more effective. 35

T
he  promise  of  anti-angiogenic  therapy  has  spurred  considerable  research  to  define  the  key  chemical

mediators  of  neovascularization.  Multiple 
factors 
are  now  known 
to  be 
capable  of  promoting
neovascularization.  These  factors  include  VEGF,  bFGF,  IL6,  IL8,  angiopoietin,  TNF-α,  MMPs  such  as
MMP-9, HIF-1α, Ephrin A1, ETS-1, Id1/Id3 and PDGF. There are also many endogenous inhibitors of

angiogenesis  such  as 
thrombospondin,  vasostatin,  various  TIMPs  and  kininogen.36  The  extent  of
neovascularization is now believed to be the result of the balance between the angiogenic promoters and
inhibitors.

o  date,  no  agent  is  known  to  influence  all  aspects  of  the  complex  angiogenesis  process:  proteolytic

cell  proliferation,  cellular  alignment  and  finally,  new  vessel  formation.  However,  several  recently

preview_rows.0: S1P is a Growth Factors for Neovascularization
The angiogenic effects of S1P are comparable to that of well-known angiogenic factors such as bFGF and
VEGF.  Furthermore  it  has  been  shown  that  S1P  elicits  a  synergic  effect  with  these  growth  factors
promote development of vascular network in vivo. S1P markedly enhances the angiogenic response in the
avascular mouse cornea to bFGF. Vascular structures resulting from the exposition of both bFGF and S1P
was  found  more  developed  that  those  obtained  from  the  exposure  to  bFGF  alone.  Recently,  cross  talk
between S1P and VEGF signaling pathways in the endothelial cells was reported. VEGF is responsible of
the up-regulation of S1P receptors in endothelial cells and acts to sensitize the vascular endothelium to the
action of S1P while S1P stimulated production of sphingosine kinase (SPHK), an enzyme responsible for
production of S1P. The treatment of endothelial cells with VEGF markedly induced the up-regulation of
S1P receptor isoform expression and enhanced S1P-mediated signaling pathways leading to the activation
of  the  endothelial  isoform  of  endothelial  nitric  oxide  synthetase  (eNOS).  It  has  been  demonstrated  that
eNOS activity plays a crucial role in different cellular responses and several essential vascular functions
including  angiogenesis,  likely  by  protecting  endothelial  cells  from  apoptosis  induced  by  migration-
induced stress.

preview_rows.0: DISCUSSION

T
he ability of LT1002 to block FGF- and VEGF-stimulated neovascularization was evaluated in the

murine  Matrigel  plug  model. 
  Animals 
treated  with  25  mg/kg  LT1002  exhibited  a  statistically
significant  reduction  in  microcapillary densities  in  VEGF-stimulated  Matrigel  plugs  when compared
to  plugs  from  saline-treated  animals.      Animals  treated  with  25  mg/kg  LT1002  but  not  1  mg/kg
LT1002  exhibited  a  non-statistical  reduction  in  microcapillary  densities  in  FGF-stimulated  Matrigel
plugs when compared to plugs from saline-treated animals.
The  mechanism  for  the  anti-tumorigenic  effects  of  LT1002  is  by  neutralization  of  S1P  by  selective
absorption.    This  ‘molecular  sponge’  concept  is  similar  to  the  mechanism  of  action  of  Avastin,  a
humanized  mAb  directed  against  the  pro-angiogenic  growth  factor,  VEGF.    In  contrast  to  the  anti-
VEGF  sponge,  most  FDA-approved  anti-cancer  therapeutic  antibodies  are  directed  against  tumor-
selective  antigens  expressed  on  the  surfaces  of  transformed  cells.    These  therapeutic  antibodies  are
often  conjugated  to  radionucliotides  or  other  toxic  materials  and  deliver  the  materials  to  tumors  by
molecular  targeting.    The  efficacy  of  this  treatment  depends,  in  part,  by  the  accessibility  of  the
antibodies to the tumor cells.  As is the case for Avastin, LT1002 used here may not suffer from this
limitation  in  that  the  target  (i.e.,  S1P)  is  circulating  in  the  same  compartment,  i.e.,  blood,  as  is  the
antibody.  Further, S1P is a lipid target that is thought to freely cross cell and compartment boundaries
more easily than protein targets like VEGF.  An additional potential advantage of LT1002 is that the
target  is  not  species-specific,  as  is  the  case  with  protein  antigens.    S1P  has  the  same  chemical
composition not only across species, but across phyla, and it is not susceptible to mutation as a means
of escaping the therapeutic.

R
educing 
the  effective  extracellular  S1P  concentration  with  LT1002  may  not  only  remove 
the
protective effects of extracellular S1P but may alter the rheostat in favor of ceramide and sphingosine.
Ceramide  and  sphingosine,  upstream  bioactive  lipids,    are  well-known  pro-apoptotic  intracellular
signaling molecules that can be activated in cancer cells by radiation and chemotherapeutic agents and
can promote apoptosis in B16-F10 cells.  Thus, it is possible that LT1002 could be used as an adjunct
to standard chemotherapy or radiation therapy.

S
elective  absorption  of  S1P  by  a  neutralizing  antibody  could  represent  a  novel  approach  to  cancer
therapy that may have distinct advantages over other targets in the sphingolipid signaling cascade (e.g.
targeting  intracellular  components  like  SPHK).    The  pleiotropic  effects  of  S1P  in  promoting  tumor
growth and angiogenesis make S1P a robust target for novel anti-cancer therapy, because there appears
to be many S1P-dependent tumor types and more than one mechanism of S1P action.  The molecular
sponge approach, coupled to the finding that antibodies have favorable pharmacokinetic features and
high  therapeutic  indices,  suggest  that  LT1002  may  provide  therapeutic  benefit  in  treating  cancer.

Clinical 
trials  however,  with  a  humanized  version  of  LT1002  will  be  needed 
to  confirm 
this
suggestion.

summary.summary: {'summary': "LT1002, a murine monoclonal antibody targeting sphingosine 1-phosphate (S1P), was evaluated for its anti-angiogenic efficacy in female C57BL/6 mice using a Matrigel plug model supplemented with FGF or VEGF. summary.summary: {'summary': 'This non-GLP study evaluated the effects of LT1002, an anti-sphingosine 1-phosphate murine monoclonal antibody, on basal and VEGF-induced epidermal vascular permeability in female nude mice using the murine Miles assay. Mice were administered 25 mg/kg LT1002 or a non-specific isotype-matched control antibody every other day via intraperitoneal injection. Vascular permeability was assessed by Evans blue dye leakage following subdermal injections of saline or human VEGF at 50 or 400 ng/mL. Results showed that LT1002 did not alter basal or VEGF-induced vascular permeability compared to control. The study supports that systemic LT1002 administration does not affect vascular permeability in this model.', 'topics': [{'topic': 'Study Objective and Design', 'summary': 'The study aimed to assess whether LT1002 could mitigate VEGF-induced increases in vascular permeability and whether LT1002 alone affects basal permeability. Female nude mice were treated with 25 mg/kg LT1002 or a non-specific monoclonal antibody every other day by intraperitoneal injection. Vascular permeability was measured using the murine Miles assay with Evans blue dye following subdermal injections of saline or VEGF.'}, {'topic': 'Materials and Methods', 'summary': 'Five to seven week old female HSD athymic nude mice were used. LT1002 and a non-specific isotype-matched control antibody (LT1011) were administered intraperitoneally. VEGF doses of 50 and 400 ng/mL were selected for subdermal injections to induce vascular permeability. Evans blue dye was injected intravenously, and dye leakage was quantified by measuring the area of dye extravasation using image analysis software.'}, {'topic': 'Results', 'summary': 'VEGF induced a dose-dependent increase in vascular permeability in both LT1002 and control antibody-treated mice. LT1002 administration did not significantly alter basal vascular permeability or VEGF-induced permeability compared to the non-specific antibody. Statistical analysis confirmed no significant differences between treatment groups.'}, {'topic': 'Discussion', 'summary': 'The findings indicate that LT1002 does not increase vascular permeability, an important safety consideration for its potential use in treating choroidal neovascularization associated with age-related macular degeneration. The study supports the hypothesis that LT1002 can neutralize extracellular S1P without adversely affecting vascular barrier function.'}, {'topic': 'Conclusion', 'summary': 'Systemic administration of LT1002 at 25 mg/kg every other day by intraperitoneal injection does not alter basal or VEGF-induced epidermal vascular permeability in female nude mice as measured by the murine Miles assay.'}]}

summary.summary: {'summary': "LT1002, a murine monoclonal antibody targeting sphingosine 1-phosphate (S1P), significantly inhibits S1P-induced migration of human umbilical vein endothelial cells (HUVECs) in vitro. Using modified Boyden chamber assays with Matrigel and vitronectin matrices, S1P was shown to increase HUVEC migration up to 4.8-fold compared to non-treated controls. Treatment with LT1002 reduced this migration to near baseline levels, demonstrating potent neutralization of S1P activity. These findings support LT1002's potential as an anti-angiogenic agent by blocking S1P-mediated endothelial cell migration, a key process in tumor angiogenesis and metastasis. The study was conducted under non-GLP conditions and utilized multiple independent experiments with statistical validation.", 'topics': [{'topic': 'Introduction and Rationale', 'summary': 'Sphingosine 1-phosphate (S1P) is a bioactive lipid involved in tumor growth, angiogenesis, and metastasis by promoting endothelial cell migration and survival. LT1002 is a murine monoclonal antibody developed to neutralize extracellular S1P, potentially reducing tumor vascularization and growth. Targeting S1P offers a novel therapeutic approach analogous to anti-VEGF strategies.'}, {'topic': 'Materials and Methods', 'summary': 'Human umbilical vein endothelial cells (HUVECs) were cultured and used between passages 3 and 8. Migration assays employed modified Boyden chambers coated with Matrigel or vitronectin matrices. Cells were treated with S1P (100 nM or 1 µM) with or without LT1002 (1 µg/mL) for 6 hours. Migrated cells were stained and counted microscopically. Data were normalized to non-treated controls and analyzed using ANOVA with Bonferroni correction.'}, {'topic': 'Results', 'summary': "S1P significantly increased HUVEC migration through both Matrigel and vitronectin matrices, with fold increases ranging from 2.2 to 4.8 over controls. LT1002 treatment markedly inhibited this migration, reducing it to near baseline levels. Statistical analysis confirmed the significance of LT1002's inhibitory effect (p<0.007). Data were consistent across four independent experiments for Matrigel and two for vitronectin."}, {'topic': 'Discussion', 'summary': "The study demonstrates LT1002's capacity to neutralize S1P-induced endothelial cell migration, suggesting a novel anti-angiogenic mechanism for cancer therapy. LT1002 acts as a 'molecular sponge' similar to Avastin's neutralization of VEGF but targets a lipid mediator with conserved structure across species. This approach may overcome limitations of tumor-targeted antibodies and offers potential advantages in pharmacokinetics and resistance."}, {'topic': 'Conclusion', 'summary': 'LT1002 effectively neutralizes S1P-induced migration of endothelial cells in vitro, supporting its development as a therapeutic agent to inhibit tumor angiogenesis. Further clinical evaluation of a humanized LT1002 is warranted to confirm its anti-cancer potential.'}]}

summary.summary: {'summary': 'Lpath, Inc. developed a murine monoclonal antibody LT1002 (Sphingomab™) targeting sphingosine 1-phosphate (S1P) to inhibit choroidal neovascularization (CNV) in a laser-induced injury model in female C57BL6/J mice. LT1002 and its humanized variants (LT1004, LT1006, LT1007, LT1009) administered intravitreally significantly reduced CNV lesion volume by 50-99%, with LT1009 showing the highest efficacy (99% inhibition). Two production lots of LT1002 (SBS and PG) showed comparable activity. The study supports S1P neutralization as a promising therapeutic approach for age-related macular degeneration (AMD), potentially superior to anti-VEGF therapies by targeting multiple pathogenic pathways.', 'topics': [{'topic': 'Introduction and Rationale', 'summary': 'S1P is a signaling lipid involved in cellular proliferation, migration, and survival, implicated in AMD pathogenesis through modulation of angiogenesis, inflammation, and fibrosis. Neutralizing extracellular S1P with LT1002 may inhibit multiple maladaptive steps in CNV formation, offering advantages over current anti-VEGF therapies.'}, {'topic': 'Materials and Methods', 'summary': "Female C57BL6/J mice underwent laser-induced rupture of Bruch's membrane to induce CNV. Mice were treated with 0.5 µg of LT1002 or humanized variants via intravitreal injection, or with isotype control antibodies or saline. CNV lesion volumes were quantified by rhodamine-labeled agglutinin staining and confocal microscopy."}, {'topic': 'Results', 'summary': 'Intravitreal administration of LT1002 and humanized variants significantly reduced CNV lesion volumes compared to controls. LT1009 showed the highest inhibition (99%), followed by LT1007 (91%), LT1004 and LT1006 (~79-80%). Two LT1002 production lots (SBS and PG) demonstrated similar efficacy. Intraperitoneal administration was less effective.'}, {'topic': 'Discussion', 'summary': 'The data confirm that targeting S1P effectively inhibits CNV in a murine model of AMD. Humanized variants maintain potent activity, supporting LT1009 as a clinical candidate. The multi-targeted mechanism of S1P neutralization may provide therapeutic benefits beyond current anti-VEGF treatments.'}, {'topic': 'Conclusion', 'summary': 'All humanized anti-S1P antibodies tested were highly effective in reducing CNV lesion formation, with LT1009 being the most potent. These findings support further clinical development of LT1009 for AMD and cancer indications.'}]}

summary.summary: {'summary': "The study evaluated the cross-reactivity of the humanized monoclonal antibody LT1009 against sphingosine-1-phosphate (S1P) and a panel of 40 structurally related lipids using a competitive ELISA assay. LT1009 specifically recognized lipids containing the phosphate group on the polar head, such as S1P, sphingosylphosphorylcholine, and dihydrosphingosine-1-phosphate, but did not bind lipids lacking this group or with modifications like fatty acid addition on the sphingoid base. Epitope mapping confirmed the phosphate group as the primary antigenic determinant. The antibody's specificity supports its therapeutic development targeting S1P-mediated pathways in cancer. The study was conducted non-GLP at Lpath, Inc. using material from a 50-L bioreactor batch of LT1009.", 'topics': [{'topic': 'Study Overview and Objectives', 'summary': 'The study aimed to assess the specificity and cross-reactivity of LT1009, a humanized anti-S1P monoclonal antibody, against various lipids naturally present in biological systems. The evaluation was performed using a competitive ELISA assay to identify potential binding to lipids structurally related to S1P.'}, {'topic': 'LT1009 Characteristics and Background', 'summary': 'LT1009 is a recombinant humanized IgG1κ monoclonal antibody derived from murine LT1002, designed to bind S1P with high affinity (<0.1 nM) and improved thermal stability. S1P is a bioactive lipid involved in cell proliferation, angiogenesis, and cancer progression, making LT1009 a promising therapeutic candidate.'}, {'topic': 'Methodology - Competition ELISA Assay', 'summary': 'The cross-reactivity was assessed by a competitive binding ELISA where S1P was coated on plates, and LT1009 was pre-incubated with competing lipids at various concentrations. Binding was detected using HRP-conjugated secondary antibodies, and inhibition of signal indicated cross-reactivity.'}, {'topic': 'Results - Cross-reactivity Findings', 'summary': 'LT1009 specifically recognized lipids containing the phosphate group on the polar head, such as S1P, sphingosylphosphorylcholine, and dihydrosphingosine-1-phosphate. It did not recognize lipids lacking the phosphate group or with fatty acid additions on the sphingoid base, such as ceramide-1-phosphate. The antibody did not cross-react with other lipid classes including lysophosphatidic acid, ceramide, and various phospholipids.'}, {'topic': 'Epitope Mapping', 'summary': 'Epitope mapping using lipids with various structural modifications confirmed that LT1009 preferentially binds the phosphate group carried by the polar head of S1P. Minimal recognition was observed for phosphate ester groups attached to the sphingoid base.'}, {'topic': 'Conclusion', 'summary': "The study confirmed the high specificity of LT1009 for the phosphate group of S1P and related lipids, supporting its therapeutic potential. The antibody's selective binding profile minimizes off-target interactions with other lipids, which is advantageous for safety and efficacy."}]}

summary.summary: {'summary': 'This study characterizes the kinetics and stoichiometry of the interaction between LT1009, a humanized anti-S1P monoclonal antibody, and its ligand sphingosine 1-phosphate (S1P). Using fluorescent binding assays, mass spectrometry, and surface plasmon resonance, LT1009 was shown to bind up to four S1P molecules per antibody in a concentration-dependent manner. Binding analyses revealed two distinct affinity modes, with high- and low-affinity binding constants, indicating a biphasic interaction. In vivo pharmacokinetic studies in mice confirmed the formation of LT1009-S1P complexes with a 1:4 stoichiometric ratio. These findings support the proposed mechanism of LT1009 neutralizing S1P by forming soluble complexes, which is relevant for dosing considerations.', 'topics': [{'topic': 'Introduction and Background', 'summary': "LT1009 is a humanized monoclonal antibody derived from LT1002, targeting the bioactive lipid S1P with high affinity. S1P is a signaling lipid involved in various physiological processes and circulates in plasma bound to lipoproteins. Understanding LT1009's binding kinetics and stoichiometry with S1P is critical for elucidating its mechanism of action and optimizing therapeutic dosing."}, {'topic': 'Materials and Methods', 'summary': 'Binding interactions were assessed using fluorescent S1P-NBD assays, mass spectrometry, and surface plasmon resonance (BIAcore 2000). Pharmacokinetic studies were conducted in athymic nude mice dosed intravenously with LT1009. Immunoprecipitation assays were performed to detect LT1009-S1P complexes in plasma. Binding data were analyzed using Lineweaver-Burk, Hill, and Scatchard plots.'}, {'topic': 'In Vitro Binding Assays', 'summary': 'LT1009 solubilized S1P-NBD to form saturable complexes with a maximum binding capacity of approximately 3.6 to 3.8 S1P molecules per antibody. Hill plot analysis indicated two distinct binding modes, with initial non-cooperative binding followed by negatively cooperative binding. Scatchard analysis revealed biphasic binding with high-affinity (Kd ~5.64 µM) and low-affinity (Kd ~34.81 µM) components.'}, {'topic': 'Mass Spectrometry and Biosensor Analysis', 'summary': 'Mass spectrometric analysis of LT1002-S1P complexes confirmed a binding stoichiometry of up to 1:4 antibody to S1P molecules. Biosensor studies demonstrated that soluble S1P partially inhibited LT1009 binding to immobilized S1P surfaces, consistent with reversible binding kinetics and a maximum binding ratio of 1:4.'}, {'topic': 'In Vivo Pharmacokinetic and Immunoprecipitation Studies', 'summary': 'Following intravenous administration of LT1009 in mice, plasma concentrations of LT1009 decreased over 24 hours while S1P levels increased, suggesting complex formation. Immunoprecipitation showed that approximately 65% of plasma S1P was bound to LT1009 at 24 and 72 hours post-dose, supporting a 1:4 stoichiometric ratio of antibody to S1P in vivo.'}, {'topic': 'Conclusions', 'summary': 'LT1009 binds S1P to form soluble complexes with a stoichiometry of up to four S1P molecules per antibody. The interaction exhibits biphasic binding kinetics with distinct affinity modes. In vivo data corroborate the in vitro findings, indicating that LT1009 forms stable complexes with S1P, which is important for understanding its pharmacodynamics and guiding dosing strategies.'}]}

summary.summary: {'summary': "This non-GLP study evaluated the binding kinetics of the humanized monoclonal antibody LT1009 to sphingosine 1-phosphate (S1P) using BIACore technology. S1P was immobilized on a sensor chip at varying densities, and LT1009 binding was analyzed via a 1:1 interaction model. The antibody demonstrated strong and reproducible binding, with an affinity of approximately 50 nM on the lowest density surface, which is considered most reliable due to reduced avidity effects. The study supports LT1009's potential as a therapeutic agent targeting extracellular S1P to inhibit tumor growth and angiogenesis. Data and materials were well documented and archived.", 'topics': [{'topic': 'Introduction', 'summary': 'Sphingosine 1-phosphate (S1P) is a bioactive lysolipid involved in tumor cell proliferation, survival, and angiogenesis. The balance between S1P and its precursors ceramide/sphingosine regulates cell fate. Overexpression of sphingosine kinase (SPHK), which produces S1P, correlates with tumor aggressiveness and poor patient survival. LT1009, a humanized monoclonal antibody against S1P, is designed to neutralize extracellular S1P and potentially inhibit tumor growth.'}, {'topic': 'Materials and Methods', 'summary': 'Binding kinetics were measured using a BIACore 2000 optical biosensor. S1P-thiol was covalently coupled to a maleimide CM5 sensor chip at three densities (7, 20, and 1000 RU). LT1009 was injected in a 3-fold dilution series starting at 117 µg/mL, with duplicate measurements. Data were globally fit to a simple 1:1 interaction model. Controls included reference surfaces and blank injections. All experiments were conducted at 25ºC.'}, {'topic': 'Results', 'summary': 'LT1009 bound strongly and reproducibly to S1P surfaces. The lowest density surface data fit well to a 1:1 interaction model, yielding an affinity of approximately 51 nM. Medium and high density surfaces showed concentration-dependent binding but may be influenced by avidity effects, making the low density surface data more reliable.'}, {'topic': 'Discussion', 'summary': "The affinity of LT1009 for S1P was determined to be 51 nM using a bivalent model, which may overestimate affinity since S1P is soluble or bound to BSA and not membrane-immobilized. A monovalent model might better represent the interaction. These considerations are important for interpreting the binding data and understanding LT1009's therapeutic potential."}, {'topic': 'Conclusion', 'summary': 'LT1009 exhibits strong binding to S1P with an affinity of approximately 50 nM on the lowest density surface, supporting its potential as a therapeutic antibody to neutralize extracellular S1P and inhibit tumor growth mechanisms.'}]}

summary.summary: {'summary': 'This non-GLP study evaluated the efficacy of LT1002, a murine monoclonal antibody targeting sphingosine 1-phosphate (S1P), in inhibiting the growth of established murine Lewis lung tumors grafted in female C57BL/6 mice. Mice bearing subcutaneous tumors (50-100 mm3) were treated intraperitoneally with 50 mg/kg LT1002 or saline every other day. Tumor volumes, weights, and lung metastatic nodules were measured at study end. Results showed no statistically significant reduction in tumor growth or metastasis with LT1002 treatment compared to controls. The study concluded that systemic administration of LT1002 did not decrease progression of pre-established Lewis lung tumors in this model.', 'topics': [{'topic': 'Introduction', 'summary': 'Sphingosine 1-phosphate (S1P) is a bioactive lipid implicated in tumor growth, angiogenesis, and metastasis. LT1002 is a monoclonal antibody developed to neutralize extracellular S1P, hypothesized to reduce tumor progression by lowering S1P levels.'}, {'topic': 'Materials and Methods', 'summary': 'Female C57BL/6 mice were subcutaneously engrafted with 5x10^5 Lewis lung carcinoma cells. summary.summary: {'summary': 'LT1002, a murine monoclonal antibody targeting sphingosine 1-phosphate (S1P), was administered intraperitoneally three times per week at 20 mg/kg to female Ncr nu/nu mice bearing established orthotopic human MDA MB 468 breast carcinoma tumors. summary.summary: {'summary': 'This non-GLP study evaluated the pharmacodynamic effects of LT1009, a humanized monoclonal antibody targeting sphingosine 1-phosphate (S1P), in female nude mice bearing orthotopically grafted human ovarian SKOV3 tumors. LT1009 was administered intraperitoneally at 25 mg/kg initially and then 10 mg/kg every three days. While LT1009 treatment did not reduce tumor volume compared to saline controls, it significantly decreased circulating levels of the pro-tumorigenic cytokine IL-8 in both serum and ascites by approximately 53-56%, and reduced VEGF levels in ascites by 18%. These findings suggest LT1009 modulates tumor-associated cytokines without affecting tumor growth in this model. The study supports further investigation of LT1009 as a potential adjunct cancer therapy targeting S1P-mediated pathways.', 'topics': [{'topic': 'Study Design and Methods', 'summary': 'Female athymic nude (Ncr Nu/Nu) mice were orthotopically grafted with 3x10^6 human ovarian SKOV3 tumor cells via intraperitoneal injection. LT1009 was administered intraperitoneally at 25 mg/kg on Days 0, 1, and 4, followed by 10 mg/kg every three days until study end at Day 52. Control animals received saline on the same schedule. Tumor weights, ascites volume, and cytokine levels in serum and ascites were measured post-mortem. Cytokine concentrations (IL-6, IL-8, VEGF) were quantified by ELISA.'}, {'topic': 'Pharmacodynamic Outcomes', 'summary': 'LT1009 treatment did not significantly reduce tumor weight compared to saline controls (mean tumor weights approximately 1059 mg vs. 989 mg). However, LT1009 significantly reduced IL-8 levels in ascites by 53% and in serum by 56%, and decreased VEGF levels in ascites by 18%. IL-6 was not detected in any samples. These results indicate LT1009 effectively lowers pro-tumorigenic cytokines associated with tumor progression.'}, {'topic': 'Mechanism and Therapeutic Implications', 'summary': 'LT1009 neutralizes extracellular S1P, a bioactive lipid involved in tumor cell proliferation, survival, and angiogenesis. By lowering S1P levels, LT1009 may shift the sphingolipid rheostat towards pro-apoptotic ceramide and sphingosine, potentially sensitizing tumor cells to apoptosis. Although tumor growth was not inhibited in this study, the cytokine modulation suggests LT1009 could serve as an adjunct to chemotherapy or radiation, warranting further clinical evaluation.'}, {'topic': 'Study Conduct and Compliance', 'summary': 'The study was conducted under non-GLP conditions with appropriate animal welfare compliance, including IACUC approval and adherence to NIH guidelines. summary.summary: {'summary': 'This non-GLP study evaluated the efficacy of LT1009 (humanized) and LT1002 (murine) monoclonal antibodies targeting sphingosine-1-phosphate (S1P) in reducing the growth of established human ovarian SKOV3 tumors orthotopically grafted in female Ncr nu/nu mice. Mice were treated thrice weekly via intraperitoneal injection with 25 mg/kg LT1009, LT1002, 10 mg/kg Paclitaxel, or vehicle. Tumor growth was assessed by anatomic and dynamic contrast-enhanced MRI (DCE-MRI) one week post-treatment initiation. Both LT1009 and LT1002 significantly inhibited tumor growth compared to vehicle, with LT1002 showing comparable efficacy to Paclitaxel. The antibodies also altered tumor vascular function, suggesting a mechanism involving S1P neutralization and vascular modulation. These findings support the potential of anti-S1P antibodies as novel anti-cancer therapeutics targeting tumor growth and angiogenesis.', 'topics': [{'topic': 'Study Design and Methods', 'summary': 'Female athymic nude (Ncr nu/nu) mice were orthotopically grafted with 2x10^6 SKOV3 human ovarian carcinoma cells via intraperitoneal injection. After tumor establishment, mice were randomized into four groups (n=10 each) receiving 25 mg/kg LT1009, 25 mg/kg LT1002, 10 mg/kg Paclitaxel, or vehicle control, administered intraperitoneally three times per week. Tumor burden was assessed longitudinally by anatomic and dynamic contrast-enhanced MRI (DCE-MRI) before and one week after treatment initiation.'}, {'topic': 'Pharmacodynamics and Efficacy', 'summary': 'Both LT1009 and LT1002 significantly reduced tumor growth compared to vehicle, as measured by MRI-derived tumor weights. LT1002 demonstrated tumor growth inhibition comparable to Paclitaxel. Tumor weight increases after one week were 221% for vehicle, 126% for LT1002, 193% for LT1009, and 125% for Paclitaxel, indicating effective mitigation of tumor progression by the anti-S1P antibodies.'}, {'topic': 'Mechanism of Action', 'summary': 'The anti-tumor effects of LT1009 and LT1002 are attributed to neutralization of extracellular S1P, acting as a molecular sponge to reduce S1P-mediated tumor proliferation and angiogenesis. This mechanism is analogous to anti-VEGF therapies like Avastin but targets a lipid mediator with cross-species conservation, potentially reducing resistance. The antibodies also decreased tumor blood volume, indicating altered tumor vascular function.'}, {'topic': 'Imaging and Data Analysis', 'summary': 'Tumor weights were quantified using region of interest (ROI) analysis on MRI images, subtracting pre-treatment from post-treatment values to account for baseline variability. DCE-MRI parameters including blood volume (v_b), Ktrans, and normalized initial area under the curve (NIAUC) were analyzed, showing significant decreases with LT1002 and LT1009 treatment, supporting vascular modulation effects.'}, {'topic': 'Study Conduct and Compliance', 'summary': 'The study was conducted under non-GLP conditions at MD Anderson Cancer Center with appropriate animal welfare compliance. No formal protocol was drafted. Data and samples were archived on the Lpath server and at MD Anderson. These findings support further clinical development of anti-S1P antibodies as novel cancer therapeutics, potentially as adjuncts to chemotherapy or radiation, targeting tumor growth and angiogenesis via S1P neutralization.'}]}

summary.summary: {'summary': 'This study evaluated the antitumor efficacy of LT1009, a humanized monoclonal antibody against sphingosine 1-phosphate (S1P), alone and in combination with Avastin, in female athymic nude mice bearing orthotopically xenografted MDA-MB-231 human breast tumors. The combination of LT1009 and Avastin did not demonstrate additive or synergistic effects. summary.summary: {'summary': 'This non-GLP study evaluated the efficacy of LT1009, a humanized monoclonal antibody targeting sphingosine 1-phosphate (S1P), in inhibiting growth of established human Panc-1 pancreatic tumors grafted subcutaneously in female nude (Ncr nu/nu) mice. Mice were treated intraperitoneally with 25 mg/kg LT1009 every three days for 39 days. Tumor volume measurements showed no significant reduction in tumor growth compared to saline controls. However, LT1009 treatment significantly reduced human IL-8 levels in serum and ascites, indicating some biological activity. The study concluded that LT1009 at this dose did not affect tumor growth, suggesting higher doses may be required for efficacy.', 'topics': [{'topic': 'Study Design and Objectives', 'summary': 'The study aimed to assess the efficacy of LT1009, a humanized monoclonal antibody against S1P, in retarding growth of established human Panc-1 pancreatic tumors in female nude mice. Tumors were grafted subcutaneously and allowed to establish for 35 days before treatment initiation. LT1009 was administered intraperitoneally at 25 mg/kg every three days, with tumor growth monitored by caliper measurements.'}, {'topic': 'Materials and Methods', 'summary': 'Female athymic nude (Ncr nu/nu) mice were used, housed under controlled conditions with IACUC approval. Panc-1 human pancreatic carcinoma cells were cultured and injected subcutaneously with Matrigel. LT1009 antibody was produced in CHO cells, purified, and administered intraperitoneally. Tumor volumes were measured weekly, and at study end, tumors were harvested and weighed. Serum and ascites were collected for IL-8 analysis by ELISA.'}, {'topic': 'Results', 'summary': 'Treatment with 25 mg/kg LT1009 produced a measurable but statistically non-significant reduction in tumor volume compared to saline controls (mean tumor volume 925 ± 552 mm3 vs. 827 ± 537 mm3). However, LT1009 significantly reduced human IL-8 levels in serum and ascites, indicating biological activity. Statistical analysis by ANOVA showed no significant difference in final tumor volumes.'}, {'topic': 'Discussion', 'summary': 'The lack of significant tumor growth inhibition at 25 mg/kg suggests this dose is insufficient for efficacy in this model. S1P is implicated in tumor proliferation and angiogenesis, and LT1009’s reduction of IL-8 supports its biological effect. The study recommends repeating with higher doses (≥ 50 mg/kg) where tumor progression inhibition has been observed.'}, {'topic': 'Conclusion', 'summary': 'LT1009 at 25 mg/kg administered intraperitoneally every three days did not inhibit growth of established Panc-1 tumors in nude mice. Further studies with increased dosing are warranted to evaluate therapeutic potential.'}]}

summary.summary: {'summary': 'This non-GLP in vivo study evaluated the antitumor efficacy of LT1009 (humanized anti-S1P monoclonal antibody) and its murine parent LT1002 in an orthotopic MCF-7 human breast tumor xenograft model in female nude mice. Mice with established tumors (~100 mm3) were treated with 40 mg/kg LT1009 or LT1002 intraperitoneally every 3 days, 50 mg/kg Docetaxel intravenously once weekly, or vehicle control. Tumor volumes were measured over 32 days. Neither LT1009 nor LT1002 significantly inhibited tumor growth compared to vehicle, while Docetaxel completely suppressed tumor progression. The study noted large variability in tumor sizes and potential bias due to early sacrifice of animals with large tumors, recommending study repetition. Microvessel density analysis was pending.', 'topics': [{'topic': 'Study Design and Methods', 'summary': 'Female nude mice were orthotopically engrafted with MCF-7 human breast tumor cells in the mammary fat pad. Upon tumor establishment (~100 mm3), animals were pair-matched and randomized into four groups receiving 40 mg/kg LT1009, 40 mg/kg LT1002, 50 mg/kg Docetaxel, or vehicle. LT1009 and LT1002 were administered intraperitoneally every 3 days, Docetaxel intravenously once weekly, and vehicle intraperitoneally every 3 days. Tumor volumes were measured longitudinally by caliper.'}, {'topic': 'Pharmacodynamic Outcomes', 'summary': 'Neither LT1009 nor LT1002 demonstrated significant inhibition of tumor growth compared to vehicle control, as assessed by final tumor volumes at Day 32. Docetaxel treatment resulted in complete tumor growth suppression. Statistical analysis showed no significant differences for LT1009 or LT1002 versus vehicle, with large inter-animal variability noted.'}, {'topic': 'Data Analysis and Variability', 'summary': 'Tumor volume data exhibited high variance within treatment groups, and several animals were sacrificed early due to large tumor burden, potentially biasing results. This was particularly evident in the vehicle group where mean tumor volume decreased after animal sacrifice. The study recommends repetition to address these limitations.'}, {'topic': 'Mechanism and Rationale', 'summary': 'LT1002 and LT1009 are monoclonal antibodies targeting sphingosine 1-phosphate (S1P), a bioactive lipid implicated in tumor cell proliferation, survival, angiogenesis, and metastasis. Neutralizing extracellular S1P is hypothesized to reduce tumor growth and metastatic potential by disrupting S1P-mediated signaling.'}, {'topic': 'Conclusions and Recommendations', 'summary': 'The study concluded that LT1009 and LT1002 did not inhibit established MCF-7 tumor progression under the tested conditions, whereas Docetaxel was effective. Due to variability and potential bias, further studies are warranted. Microvessel density analysis to assess anti-angiogenic effects was pending at report completion.'}]}

summary.summary: {'summary': "This non-GLP in vivo study evaluated the antitumor efficacy of LT1009, a humanized monoclonal antibody against sphingosine 1-phosphate (S1P), compared to its murine surrogate LT1002 and cyclophosphamide in a B16-F10 murine melanoma tumor allograft model in female B6D2F1 mice. Mice bearing established subcutaneous tumors were treated intraperitoneally with 40 mg/kg LT1009 or LT1002 every three days, or a single dose of 300 mg/kg cyclophosphamide. LT1009 treatment resulted in a 25% reduction in final tumor volume compared to vehicle, whereas LT1002 showed no tumor growth inhibition. Cyclophosphamide significantly reduced tumor growth by 81%. Due to high variability in tumor volumes, the LT1009 effect was not statistically significant. The study supports LT1009's potential anti-angiogenic activity in tumor growth retardation.", 'topics': [{'topic': 'Study Objective and Design', 'summary': 'The study aimed to assess the antitumor efficacy of LT1009 compared to LT1002 and cyclophosphamide in female B6D2F1 mice bearing established subcutaneous B16-F10 melanoma tumors. Four groups of 8 mice each were treated with vehicle, 40 mg/kg LT1009, 40 mg/kg LT1002, or 300 mg/kg cyclophosphamide. Antibodies were administered intraperitoneally every three days, while cyclophosphamide was given once on Day 1. Tumor volumes were measured longitudinally to monitor growth.'}, {'topic': 'Pharmacodynamic Rationale', 'summary': 'LT1009 and LT1002 are monoclonal antibodies targeting extracellular sphingosine 1-phosphate (S1P), a bioactive lipid implicated in tumor cell proliferation, survival, and angiogenesis. The B16-F10 melanoma cells are unresponsive to S1P directly, suggesting that antibody effects are likely mediated via anti-angiogenic mechanisms rather than direct tumor cell targeting.'}, {'topic': 'Efficacy Results', 'summary': 'LT1009 treatment led to a 25% reduction in final tumor volume compared to vehicle controls, while LT1002 showed a slight increase in tumor volume (-13% reduction). Cyclophosphamide significantly inhibited tumor growth by 81%. Despite the observed tumor volume reduction with LT1009, statistical significance was not achieved due to large standard deviations across groups.'}, {'topic': 'Statistical Analysis', 'summary': "An independent ANOVA with Bonferroni correction was performed. Cyclophosphamide showed statistically significant tumor volume reduction compared to vehicle (p=0.007). LT1009's tumor volume reduction was not statistically significant (p>0.05), and LT1002 showed no significant effect. Variability in tumor sizes contributed to the lack of statistical significance for LT1009."}, {'topic': 'Conclusions and Implications', 'summary': "The study concluded that LT1009, but not LT1002, inhibited tumor progression by 25% in this murine melanoma model, supporting its potential as an anti-angiogenic cancer therapeutic. Cyclophosphamide served as a positive control confirming model responsiveness. The findings warrant further investigation of LT1009's efficacy with optimized dosing or in combination therapies."}]}

summary.summary: {'summary': 'This pilot bioassay study evaluated the bioactivity of LT1009 (humanized monoclonal antibody sonepcizumab) and its murine precursor LT1002 by measuring their ability to neutralize sphingosine 1-phosphate (S1P)-induced interleukin-8 (IL-8) release from human ovarian SKOV3 tumor cells in vitro. The study supports the feasibility of this bioassay to assess bioactivity of LT1009 drug substance and product batches, aiding clinical development for cancer treatment. The study was non-GLP and conducted at Catalent Pharma Solutions.', 'topics': [{'topic': 'Study Objective and Design', 'summary': 'The study aimed to develop and validate a bioassay to measure the bioactivity of LT1009 and LT1002 based on their ability to neutralize S1P-induced IL-8 release from human ovarian SKOV3 tumor cells. These results demonstrate the bioactivity of both antibodies and support the assay's utility."}, {'topic': 'Study Conduct and Compliance', 'summary': 'The study was conducted as a non-GLP pilot bioassay at Catalent Pharma Solutions, with no formal compliance to OECD GLP, GMP, or GCP principles. summary.summary: {'summary': "This non-GLP study evaluated the antitumor efficacy of LT1009, a humanized monoclonal antibody targeting sphingosine 1-phosphate (S1P), alone and in combination with Avastin or Paclitaxel in a DU145 human prostate tumor xenograft model in nude NCR mice. Combination treatments of LT1009 with Avastin or Paclitaxel did not significantly enhance antitumor effects beyond those of Avastin or Paclitaxel alone. summary.summary: {'summary': 'This non-GLP study evaluated the antitumor efficacy of LT1009, a humanized monoclonal antibody targeting sphingosine 1-phosphate (S1P), alone and in combination with Avastin and 5-fluorouracil (5-FU) in a human HT29 colorectal tumor xenograft model in nude NCR mice. LT1009 at 50 mg/kg reduced tumor progression by 13%, while Avastin at 20 mg/kg reduced tumor weights by 29%. The combination of LT1009 and Avastin showed a statistically significant 40% reduction in tumor weights compared to vehicle, outperforming either agent alone. Treatment with 5-FU reduced tumor weights by 28%, and its combination with LT1009 showed a 29% reduction with minimal additive effect. Microvascular density analysis was pending at study completion. Tumor growth was monitored by volume measurements and final tumor weights, with treatments administered via intraperitoneal or intravenous routes on specified schedules.', 'topics': [{'topic': 'Study Objective and Design', 'summary': 'The study aimed to assess the efficacy of LT1009 alone and in combination with Avastin and 5-FU against human HT29 colorectal tumors implanted subcutaneously in female athymic NCr-nu/nu mice. Treatments were initiated when tumors reached 100-200 mm3, with LT1009 administered intraperitoneally every two days (first dose intravenous), Avastin intravenously every four days, and 5-FU intraperitoneally every four days. Tumor growth was monitored by measuring tumor dimensions and calculating volumes.'}, {'topic': 'Pharmacodynamic Outcomes', 'summary': 'LT1009 monotherapy reduced tumor weights by 13%, Avastin by 29%, and 5-FU by 28% compared to vehicle controls. The combination of LT1009 and Avastin significantly enhanced efficacy, achieving a 40% reduction in tumor weights (p<0.001). The combination of LT1009 and 5-FU showed a 29% reduction with minimal additive effect. Statistical analyses confirmed the significance of these findings.'}, {'topic': 'Mechanism and Rationale', 'summary': 'LT1009 is a humanized monoclonal antibody targeting sphingosine 1-phosphate (S1P), a bioactive lipid implicated in tumor cell proliferation, survival, angiogenesis, and metastasis. Neutralizing extracellular S1P is hypothesized to reduce tumor growth and vascularization by disrupting S1P-mediated signaling pathways.'}, {'topic': 'Tumor Measurement and Analysis', 'summary': 'Tumor volumes were calculated using an ellipsoid formula based on three-axis measurements, assuming unit density. summary.summary: {'summary': 'This study evaluated the efficacy of LT1002, a murine monoclonal antibody against sphingosine 1-phosphate (S1P), and its humanized form LT1009 in inhibiting the growth of human ovarian (SKOV3) tumor xenografts in female nude mice. Mice bearing established subcutaneous SKOV3 tumors were treated with 25 mg/kg LT1002 or LT1009 intraperitoneally every three days, 15 mg/kg Paclitaxel intravenously daily for five days, or vehicle control. While LT1002 and LT1009 did not significantly reduce tumor volume compared to control, both antibodies significantly decreased tumor microvascular density (MVD) by 25-35%, indicating anti-angiogenic activity. Paclitaxel treatment significantly reduced both tumor volume and MVD. These findings suggest LT1009 and LT1002 may inhibit tumor angiogenesis but not tumor growth in this model, supporting further investigation as adjunct cancer therapies targeting S1P-mediated pathways.', 'topics': [{'topic': 'Study Design and Methods', 'summary': 'Human SKOV3 ovarian tumor fragments were engrafted subcutaneously into female nude mice. After tumors reached approximately 100 mm3, mice were treated with LT1002 or LT1009 (25 mg/kg, intraperitoneal, every 3 days), Paclitaxel (15 mg/kg, intravenous, daily for 5 days), or vehicle control. Tumor volumes were measured longitudinally, and at study end, tumors were harvested for microvascular density (MVD) analysis by CD-31 staining.'}, {'topic': 'Tumor Growth Results', 'summary': 'Neither LT1002 nor LT1009 significantly inhibited tumor growth compared to vehicle control, with final tumor volumes around 1400-1450 mm3 across groups. In contrast, Paclitaxel treatment markedly reduced tumor volume to approximately 60 mm3, demonstrating expected efficacy.'}, {'topic': 'Microvascular Density Findings', 'summary': 'Both LT1002 and LT1009 treatments significantly reduced tumor microvascular density by 25% and 35%, respectively, compared to control (p<0.01 and p<0.0001). Paclitaxel also significantly decreased MVD by 56% (p<0.0001), indicating strong anti-angiogenic effects of all active treatments.'}, {'topic': 'Mechanistic Insights and Discussion', 'summary': 'S1P is implicated in tumor proliferation and angiogenesis. Neutralizing extracellular S1P with LT1009 may disrupt tumor-supportive signaling and shift the balance toward pro-apoptotic sphingolipids. Although no tumor growth inhibition was observed, the significant MVD reduction suggests potential utility of LT1009 as an adjunct to chemotherapy or radiation by targeting tumor angiogenesis.'}, {'topic': 'Conclusions', 'summary': 'LT1002 and LT1009 did not reduce SKOV3 tumor growth but significantly decreased tumor angiogenesis in a nude mouse xenograft model. These results support further development of LT1009 as a novel anti-angiogenic cancer therapeutic targeting S1P.'}]}

summary.summary: {'summary': "This report details computational modeling and docking studies of anti-S1P antibodies, including a mouse monoclonal antibody and its humanized variant. Using Sapient Discovery's Augmented Homology ModelingTM (AHM) methodology, structural models of the antibody variable domains were generated and refined. Docking studies identified multiple potential S1P binding sites at the antigen-binding region, with key residues such as Arg55L2, Lys59H2, and Arg65H2 involved in hydrogen bonding with the S1P phosphate group. Electrostatic surface analyses revealed negatively charged patches unfavorable for S1P binding, but positively charged clusters at the VL:VH interface likely facilitate ligand interaction. The study suggests that two S1P molecules can bind simultaneously at distinct sites, stabilized by hydrophobic interactions, and proposes further mutational and crystallographic studies to refine antibody design and understand binding mechanisms.", 'topics': [{'topic': 'Modeling Methodology', 'summary': "Sapient Discovery's Augmented Homology ModelingTM (AHM) was employed to generate and refine structural models of mouse and humanized anti-S1P antibody variable domains. The method includes sequence alignment, loop modeling with a modified ECEPP procedure, and refinement via molecular mechanics, dynamics, and simulated annealing, ensuring stereochemical and energetic quality suitable for docking studies."}, {'topic': 'Antibody Sequences and Variants', 'summary': 'The study used mouse monoclonal antibody M306D and several humanized variants generated by Lpath Therapeutics. Humanization involved selecting human frameworks while retaining mouse CDRs, with vernier back mutations introduced to restore key residues for CDR geometry and binding affinity. The final humanized variant S1PRHB x S1PRKK showed binding affinity comparable to the mouse antibody.'}, {'topic': 'Docking and Binding Site Identification', 'summary': 'Docking of S1P to antibody models identified three potential binding sites within the antigen-binding region, with the phosphate head interacting primarily with positively charged residues such as Arg55L2, Lys59H2, and Arg65H2. Monte Carlo simulations and energy minimizations refined these complexes, revealing hydrophobic crevices accommodating the S1P tail and multiple hydrogen bonds stabilizing the interactions.'}, {'topic': 'Electrostatic and Structural Analysis', 'summary': "Electrostatic surface mapping showed a negatively charged patch at CDR L1, unfavorable for S1P binding, but positively charged clusters at the VL:VH interface likely attract the ligand. Structural superpositions revealed conformational differences in CDR loops, especially H3, between Sapient and Lpath models, affecting residue accessibility such as Arg55L2, which is solvent-exposed in Sapient models but buried in Lpath's."}, {'topic': 'Binding Energies and Interaction Details', 'summary': 'Binding energy calculations indicated similar affinities for mouse and humanized antibody-S1P complexes across docking sites. Hydrogen bonding and van der Waals contacts involve key residues in CDR loops, with hydrophobic interactions between S1P tails contributing to complex stability. Mutation studies highlighted residues like Ser49L as critical for structural stability and binding.'}, {'topic': 'Conclusions and Future Directions', 'summary': 'The study concludes that multiple S1P molecules can bind simultaneously to the antibody at distinct sites, stabilized by electrostatic and hydrophobic interactions. Vernier back mutations enhance structural stability of CDR loops. Future work includes X-ray crystallography to precisely define antibody-S1P interactions and guide antibody engineering for improved therapeutic efficacy.'}]}

summary.summary: {'summary': "The humanized monoclonal antibody LT1009 specifically binds the bioactive lipid sphingosine-1-phosphate (S1P) with a stoichiometry of up to four S1P molecules per antibody. Binding occurs via a biphasic, negatively cooperative mechanism, supported by fluorescence and mass spectrometry data. Molecular modeling identified three distinct S1P binding sites within the Fab variable domain, with key charged residues mediating electrostatic and hydrogen bonding interactions. Site-directed mutagenesis of these residues significantly reduced S1P binding, confirming their functional importance. summary.summary: {'summary': 'This cardiovascular and respiratory safety pharmacology study evaluated the effects of LT1009 administered via 30-minute intravenous infusion in telemetered cynomolgus monkeys. Four male monkeys received vehicle and LT1009 at doses of 10, 30, and 100 mg/kg in a Latin-square crossover design. Hemodynamic parameters, ECG intervals, respiratory rates, arterial blood gases, and core body temperature were monitored. LT1009 was well tolerated with no adverse clinical observations or changes in respiratory parameters, body temperature, or ECG intervals. The highest dose (100 mg/kg) caused a transient, non-adverse increase in blood pressure and heart rate. No mortality or moribundity was observed. The study complied with GLP standards and followed ICH S7A guidance.', 'topics': [{'topic': 'Study Design and Methods', 'summary': 'The study used four non-naïve male cynomolgus monkeys implanted with telemetry devices and vascular access ports. Hemodynamic parameters, ECGs, respiratory rates, arterial blood gases, and core body temperature were monitored before, during, and after dosing. summary.summary: {'summary': 'This GLP-compliant safety pharmacology study evaluated the cardiovascular and respiratory effects of LT1009 administered via 30-minute intravenous infusion to telemetered male cynomolgus monkeys. Four animals received vehicle and LT1009 at doses of 10, 30, and 100 mg/kg in a Latin-square crossover design. LT1009 was well tolerated with no adverse clinical signs, body weight changes, or effects on respiratory rate, arterial blood gases, body temperature, or ECG intervals. The highest dose (100 mg/kg) caused a modest, non-adverse increase in blood pressure (5-12%) lasting up to 3 hours post-infusion and a transient heart rate increase (up to 15%) between 40 and 110 minutes post-dose. Toxicokinetic analysis showed dose-proportional systemic exposure and a terminal half-life of approximately 40 hours. Overall, LT1009 demonstrated a favorable cardiovascular and respiratory safety profile in this non-human primate model.', 'topics': [{'topic': 'Study Design and Objectives', 'summary': 'The study was conducted under GLP at Charles River Laboratories using four telemetered male cynomolgus monkeys in a Latin-square crossover design. LT1009 was administered intravenously at 10, 30, and 100 mg/kg doses with vehicle control. The objective was to assess potential cardiovascular and respiratory effects relevant to human safety, including hemodynamic parameters, ECG intervals, respiratory rate, and arterial blood gases.'}, {'topic': 'Methods and Monitoring', 'summary': 'Hemodynamic parameters (systolic, diastolic, mean arterial pressure, heart rate), core body temperature, and ECGs were continuously monitored via telemetry before, during, and up to 24 hours post-dose. Respiratory rate and arterial blood gases (pH, pCO2, pO2, SO2, HCO3-) were measured at specified time points. ECG intervals (PR, QRS, QT, QTc) were quantitatively analyzed by a veterinary cardiologist.'}, {'topic': 'Cardiovascular Findings', 'summary': 'No LT1009-related changes were observed at 10 and 30 mg/kg doses. At 100 mg/kg, LT1009 caused a statistically significant but non-adverse increase in diastolic, systolic, and mean arterial blood pressures by 5-12% from 5 minutes after infusion start to approximately 3 hours post-infusion. Heart rate increased transiently by up to 15% between 40 and 110 minutes post-dose. ECG intervals showed no biologically significant alterations.'}, {'topic': 'Respiratory and Other Safety Parameters', 'summary': 'Respiratory rate and arterial blood gas parameters remained unaffected by LT1009 at all doses. Core body temperature and clinical observations showed no treatment-related changes. No adverse effects or dose-limiting toxicities were identified.'}, {'topic': 'Toxicokinetics', 'summary': 'Plasma concentrations of LT1009 increased proportionally with dose. The terminal elimination half-life was approximately 40 hours in animals where it could be determined, supporting systemic exposure consistent with the dosing regimen.'}, {'topic': 'Conclusions', 'summary': 'Intravenous LT1009 administration up to 100 mg/kg was well tolerated in cynomolgus monkeys with no adverse cardiovascular or respiratory effects. The observed increases in blood pressure and heart rate at the highest dose were not considered toxicologically meaningful, supporting the safety of LT1009 for further clinical development.'}]}

summary.summary: {'summary': 'This non-GLP study evaluated the effects of LT1002, an anti-sphingosine 1-phosphate (S1P) monoclonal antibody, on infarct size in a murine cardiac ischemia/reperfusion (I/R) model. Mice received 25 mg/kg LT1002 or control antibodies via intraperitoneal injection either 1 hour before or 48 hours after I/R injury induced by left anterior descending artery ligation. Infarct size (IS) and area at risk (AAR) were assessed after 4 days of reperfusion using Evans Blue and TTC staining. Pre-treatment with LT1002 did not significantly affect AAR or IS compared to non-specific antibody controls. Post-treatment with LT1002 showed a slight but statistically significant increase in IS/AAR ratio compared to non-specific antibody controls, while no significant difference was observed versus PBS controls. Overall, LT1002 had limited impact on myocardial damage and infarct size in this model.', 'topics': [{'topic': 'Study Design and Methods', 'summary': 'The study used male C57BL/6J mice subjected to 30 minutes of left anterior descending artery ligation followed by 4 days of reperfusion. LT1002 or control antibodies (non-specific mAb or PBS) were administered intraperitoneally at 25 mg/kg either 1 hour before or 48 hours after ischemic insult. Infarct size and area at risk were quantified using Evans Blue dye and TTC staining, with digital image analysis performed blinded to treatment.'}, {'topic': 'Pharmacological Background', 'summary': 'Sphingosine 1-phosphate (S1P) is a bioactive lipid involved in cardiovascular function and myocardial cell survival. Previous studies indicate S1P can be cardioprotective by reducing hypoxia-induced cell death. LT1002 is an anti-S1P antibody designed to scavenge circulating and local S1P, potentially modulating cardiac response to ischemia.'}, {'topic': 'Results - Pre-treatment Effects', 'summary': 'Administration of LT1002 1 hour prior to ischemia did not significantly alter the size of the area at risk or infarct size compared to non-specific antibody controls. Statistical analysis showed no significant differences in AAR/LV or IS/AAR ratios between LT1002 and control groups.'}, {'topic': 'Results - Post-treatment Effects', 'summary': 'Treatment with LT1002 48 hours after ischemic insult resulted in a modest but statistically significant increase in the IS/AAR ratio compared to non-specific antibody controls, indicating a slight increase in infarct size relative to the area at risk. No significant differences were observed when compared to PBS-treated controls.'}, {'topic': 'Discussion and Conclusion', 'summary': 'The study suggests that LT1002 has limited effects on myocardial infarct size in the murine I/R model. While pre-treatment showed no impact, post-treatment slightly increased infarct size relative to controls. The clinical relevance of these findings remains uncertain, and the ability of LT1002 to modulate cardiac cell survival via S1P scavenging may have only modest effects in this context.'}, {'topic': 'Analytical and Statistical Data', 'summary': 'Detailed quantitative data including individual animal infarct and area at risk measurements were provided. Statistical analyses using ANOVA indicated no significant differences in AAR/LV or LV weight between groups, but a significant difference in IS/AAR was observed post-treatment. Certificates of analysis confirmed the purity and potency of LT1002 and control antibodies.'}]}

summary.summary: {'summary': 'A 28-day intravenous injection toxicity study with a 28-day recovery period was conducted in Cynomolgus monkeys to evaluate the immunogenicity of LT1009, a humanized monoclonal antibody targeting sphingosine 1-phosphate (S1P). The study involved dosing at 0, 3, 10, 30, and 100 mg/kg with subsequent measurement of anti-LT1009 antibodies using a competitive antibody binding ELISA (CABE). Immunogenic responses increased dose-dependently, with no responses in control animals and full response at the highest dose by Day 57. Polyclonal anti-LT1009 antibodies were developed in rabbits as positive controls. The study complied with GLP and supported clinical development plans for LT1009 in cancer therapy.', 'topics': [{'topic': 'Study Design and Conduct', 'summary': 'LT1009 was administered intravenously to male and female Cynomolgus monkeys at doses of 0, 3, 10, 30, and 100 mg/kg three times weekly for 28 days, followed by a 28-day recovery period. Blood samples were collected at multiple time points for immunogenicity analysis. The study was conducted under GLP conditions at LAB Research, Inc., with bioanalytical testing performed by Catalent, Inc.'}, {'topic': 'Immunogenicity Assessment Methodology', 'summary': 'Immunogenicity was assessed using a competitive antibody binding ELISA (CABE) that detects neutralizing anti-LT1009 antibodies by measuring inhibition of LT1009 binding to S1P. Polyclonal anti-LT1009 antibodies were generated in rabbits to serve as positive controls and to establish assay cut-offs.'}, {'topic': 'Immunogenicity Results', 'summary': 'Immunogenic responses increased with LT1009 dose, with no responses in control animals. By Day 57, 0/4, 0/4, 2/4, 3/4, and 4/4 animals showed positive anti-LT1009 antibody responses at 0, 3, 10, 30, and 100 mg/kg doses, respectively. Background subtraction analysis confirmed dose-dependent immunogenicity.'}, {'topic': 'Clinical Development Context', 'summary': 'LT1009 (ASONEP™) is a humanized IgG1κ monoclonal antibody targeting S1P, intended for cancer treatment in combination with cytotoxic and anti-angiogenic agents. The immunogenicity data support planned Phase 1 clinical trials to establish safety, tolerability, pharmacokinetics, and immunogenicity in patients with advanced refractory solid tumors.'}, {'topic': 'Data Management and Compliance', 'summary': 'All study data, protocols, and reports are archived for at least three years at LAB Research, Catalent, and indefinitely at Lpath, Inc. summary.summary: {'summary': 'The study evaluated the potential of LT1009, a humanized anti-S1P monoclonal antibody, to stimulate cytokine release from human whole blood in vitro using a multiplex Luminex assay. Cytokines measured included IL-1β, IL-2, IL-4, IL-6, IL-8, IL-10, IFN-γ, TNF-α, and GM-CSF. Results showed no significant cytokine release induced by LT1009 at any concentration compared to controls, indicating no pro-inflammatory cytokine stimulation. This supports the safety profile of LT1009 regarding cytokine release in human blood. summary.summary: {'summary': "A non-GLP study was conducted at Charles River Laboratories to quantitatively determine the concentrations of cytokines IL-1β, IL-2, IL-4, IL-6, IL-8, IL-10, IFN-γ, TNF-α, and GM-CSF in human plasma using a multiplex Luminex method. Samples originated from an in vitro evaluation of LT1009's influence on human whole blood hemolysis and plasma flocculation, involving six donors divided into control and LT1009-treated groups. Cytokine levels in treated groups were comparable to or below those in control groups, with no test article-related changes or trends observed. summary.summary: {'summary': 'This GLP-compliant study evaluated the effect of LT1002, a murine monoclonal antibody against sphingosine 1-phosphate, on wound healing in male CD-1 mice following daily intraperitoneal injections for up to 14 days. Three dose groups (PBS control, LT1002 at 30 and 90 mg/kg/day) and a positive control (dexamethasone 8 mg/kg/day, subcutaneous) were assessed for clinical signs, body weight, coagulation, histopathology, and wound tensile strength. LT1002 showed no adverse effects on clinical parameters or coagulation and demonstrated wound healing efficiency comparable to PBS control at both dose levels, while dexamethasone impaired healing. Histopathology confirmed similar reparative changes in LT1002 and control groups, and tensile strength measurements supported these findings, with some variability noted. Analytical testing confirmed LT1002 dosing formulations contained 70-83% of nominal concentrations. Overall, LT1002 did not adversely affect wound healing and was as effective as vehicle control in this model.', 'topics': [{'topic': 'Study Design and Test Articles', 'summary': 'The study involved male CD-1 mice assigned to four groups: PBS vehicle control, dexamethasone positive control (8 mg/kg/day, subcutaneous), and LT1002 at 30 or 90 mg/kg/day administered intraperitoneally daily for 14 days. Six animals per group were sacrificed on Days 4, 8, and 14 for assessments. LT1002 is a murine monoclonal antibody targeting sphingosine 1-phosphate, formulated at 6 and 18 mg/mL. Dosing volumes were 5 mL/kg for LT1002 and PBS, and 4 mL/kg for dexamethasone.'}, {'topic': 'In-Life Observations and Clinical Pathology', 'summary': 'No mortality related to treatment was observed except for three animals replaced due to poor condition. Clinical signs were not adversely affected by LT1002 at either dose. Body weights remained stable in LT1002 groups, while dexamethasone-treated animals showed reduced body weight by Day 14. Coagulation parameters (prothrombin time and activated partial thromboplastin time) showed no toxicologically significant changes with LT1002, whereas dexamethasone increased coagulation times on Day 14.'}, {'topic': 'Histopathology and Wound Healing Assessment', 'summary': 'Histopathological examination revealed full-thickness skin incisions involving epidermis, dermis, and subcutaneous tissues in all groups. LT1002 at both dose levels demonstrated wound healing efficiency comparable to PBS control across all time points. Dexamethasone-treated mice exhibited attenuated inflammatory and proliferative phases, indicating less efficient healing. Reparative changes in subcutaneous muscle and connective tissue were consistent with expected healing processes. Wound neo-vascularization was minimal in all groups.'}, {'topic': 'Tensile Strength Testing', 'summary': 'Wound tensile strength was measured on skin samples from the cranial wound section using a biomechanical tester. On Days 8 and 14, tensile strength values showed high intergroup variability but generally indicated comparable healing between PBS control and LT1002 at 30 mg/kg/day. Dexamethasone and LT1002 at 90 mg/kg/day groups had slightly lower tensile strength. Day 4 tensile strength results were inconclusive relative to histopathology.'}, {'topic': 'Analytical and Quality Assurance', 'summary': 'Dosing formulations of LT1002 were analyzed by ELISA, confirming concentrations at approximately 70% and 83% of nominal for 6 and 18 mg/mL formulations, respectively. The study was conducted in compliance with GLP regulations, with quality assurance audits performed at LAB Research Inc. and Bio Syntech Canada Inc. All data, protocols, and reports are archived per regulatory requirements.'}]}

summary.summary: {'summary': 'This GLP-compliant study evaluated the safety pharmacology of LT1002, an anti-sphingosine 1-phosphate murine monoclonal antibody, on wound healing and coagulation in male CD-1 mice. Mice received intraperitoneal injections of LT1002 at 0, 30, or 90 mg/kg/day for up to 14 days, with dexamethasone as a positive control. LT1002 showed no treatment-related adverse effects on mortality, clinical signs, body weight, coagulation parameters, necropsy, or histopathology of wound sites. Although minor, non-statistically significant reductions in wound tensile strength were observed at some time points, LT1002 was as effective as vehicle in supporting wound healing. Overall, LT1002 administration did not impair coagulation or histological wound healing in this model.', 'topics': [{'topic': 'Study Design and Objectives', 'summary': 'The study assessed the effects of LT1002 administered intraperitoneally at 0, 30, or 90 mg/kg/day for 14 days on wound healing and coagulation in male CD-1 mice. A positive control group received dexamethasone subcutaneously. Each mouse received a 3 cm full-thickness cutaneous incision prior to dosing. Evaluations included mortality, clinical signs, body weight, coagulation parameters, necropsy, histopathology, and tensile strength of wound tissue.'}, {'topic': 'Clinical Observations and Mortality', 'summary': 'No premature deaths or treatment-related adverse clinical signs were observed in LT1002-treated groups. Body weights remained unaffected by LT1002, whereas dexamethasone-treated mice showed reduced body weights by Day 14.'}, {'topic': 'Coagulation and Necropsy Findings', 'summary': 'Coagulation parameters, including prothrombin time (PT) and activated partial thromboplastin time (APTT), showed no adverse treatment-related changes with LT1002. A statistically significant reduction in APTT was noted on Day 8 at 90 mg/kg but was considered incidental. Necropsy revealed no treatment-related abnormalities.'}, {'topic': 'Histopathology and Wound Healing Efficiency', 'summary': 'Histopathological examination confirmed full-thickness incisions in all animals. LT1002 at both dose levels demonstrated wound healing efficiency comparable to vehicle controls at all time points. Dexamethasone-treated animals exhibited less efficient wound healing.'}, {'topic': 'Tensile Strength Analysis', 'summary': 'Tensile strength of wound tissue was reduced in dexamethasone-treated mice at all time points. LT1002 treatment showed minor, non-statistically significant reductions in tensile strength at 30 mg/kg on Day 4 and at 90 mg/kg on Days 8 and 14. Data variability was high, and no significant impairment of wound strength was concluded.'}, {'topic': 'Conclusion', 'summary': 'LT1002 administered intraperitoneally at 30 and 90 mg/kg/day for up to 14 days did not adversely affect coagulation or histological wound healing in male CD-1 mice. summary.summary: {'summary': 'This non-GLP study evaluated the effects of LT1002, an anti-sphingosine 1-phosphate murine monoclonal antibody, on basal and VEGF-induced vascular permeability in female nude mice using the murine Miles assay. Mice were administered 25 mg/kg LT1002 or a non-specific isotype-matched control antibody every other day via intraperitoneal injection. Vascular permeability was assessed by Evans Blue dye leakage following subdermal injections of saline or VEGF at 50 and 400 ng/mL. Results showed that VEGF induced a dose-dependent increase in vascular permeability, but LT1002 treatment did not alter basal or VEGF-induced permeability compared to control. The study concluded that systemic LT1002 administration does not affect vascular permeability in this model.', 'topics': [{'topic': 'Study Objective and Design', 'summary': 'The study aimed to assess whether LT1002 could mitigate VEGF-induced vascular permeability and whether LT1002 alone affects basal permeability. Female nude mice were treated with 25 mg/kg LT1002 or a non-specific monoclonal antibody every other day by intraperitoneal injection, followed by subdermal injections of saline or VEGF. Vascular permeability was measured using the Miles assay with Evans Blue dye leakage.'}, {'topic': 'Materials and Methods', 'summary': 'Five to seven-week-old female HSD athymic nude mice were used. LT1002 and a non-specific isotype-matched control antibody (LT1011) were administered intraperitoneally. VEGF doses of 50 and 400 ng/mL were selected for subdermal injections. Evans Blue dye was injected intravenously, and dye leakage was quantified by measuring the area of dye extravasation using image analysis software.'}, {'topic': 'Results', 'summary': 'VEGF induced a dose-dependent increase in vascular permeability as expected. However, LT1002 treatment did not significantly alter basal vascular permeability or VEGF-induced permeability compared to the non-specific antibody control. Statistical analysis confirmed no significant differences between LT1002 and control groups.'}, {'topic': 'Conclusion', 'summary': 'Systemic administration of LT1002 at 25 mg/kg every other day by intraperitoneal injection does not affect basal or VEGF-induced vascular permeability in female nude mice as measured by the Miles assay.'}, {'topic': 'Compliance and Study Conduct', 'summary': 'The study was conducted as a non-GLP research protocol, with no deviations from the protocol. Animal care complied with USDA and ILAR guidelines, and all procedures were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC).'}]}

summary.summary: {'summary': 'An in vitro study was conducted to evaluate the influence of LT1009 on human whole blood hemolysis and plasma flocculation. Whole blood samples from six healthy adults (3 males, 3 females) were spiked with LT1009 at concentrations of 43, 140, and 421 µg/mL, alongside appropriate negative and positive controls. Hemolysis was assessed by measuring whole blood hematocrit, hemoglobin concentrations, plasma hemolytic index, and visual inspection, while flocculation was evaluated by plasma turbidity index and visual assessment. summary.summary: {'summary': 'This non-GLP safety pharmacology study evaluated the effect of LT1002, a murine anti-sphingosine 1-phosphate monoclonal antibody, on vascular permeability in male CD-1 mice following four consecutive days of intraperitoneal administration at doses of 0, 30, and 90 mg/kg. Vascular permeability was assessed using Evans Blue dye extravasation and spectrophotometric analysis of formamide-extracted tissues from multiple organs. No significant differences in vascular permeability or organ weights were observed between LT1002-treated and vehicle control groups, while the positive control (interleukin-2) induced increased vascular permeability. The no-observable effect level for vascular permeability was established at 90 mg/kg/day. These results support the vascular safety profile of LT1002 under the tested conditions.', 'topics': [{'topic': 'Study Design', 'summary': 'Male CD-1 mice were dosed once daily via intraperitoneal injection for four consecutive days with LT1002 at 0, 30, or 90 mg/kg. A positive control group received interleukin-2 (1,500,000 IU) three times daily. On Day 4, Evans Blue dye was administered intravenously, and animals were euthanized two hours later for tissue collection and analysis.'}, {'topic': 'Methods of Vascular Permeability Assessment', 'summary': 'Vascular permeability was evaluated by measuring the optical density of formamide-extracted Evans Blue dye from selected organs including colon, kidney, brain, heart, liver, lungs, spleen, small intestine, and lymph nodes. Whole-body perfusion was performed prior to tissue collection to remove intravascular dye.'}, {'topic': 'Results', 'summary': 'No mortality or adverse clinical signs were observed in LT1002-treated animals. Organ weights and vascular permeability measurements showed no statistically significant differences between LT1002 and vehicle groups. The positive control group exhibited increased vascular permeability and organ weight changes consistent with vascular leakage.'}, {'topic': 'Statistical Analysis', 'summary': 'ANOVA with Bonferroni post-hoc tests confirmed no significant increase in vascular permeability in LT1002-treated groups compared to vehicle controls. Significant increases were only observed in the interleukin-2 positive control group.'}, {'topic': 'Conclusion', 'summary': 'Repeated intraperitoneal administration of LT1002 at doses up to 90 mg/kg/day for four days does not induce vascular permeability in male CD-1 mice. The no-observable effect level for vascular permeability was determined to be 90 mg/kg/day.'}]}

summary.summary: {'summary': 'A non-GLP safety pharmacology study evaluated the effect of LT1002, an anti-sphingosine 1-phosphate murine monoclonal antibody, on activated clotting time (ACT) in C57/BL6 mice. Eighteen male and female mice received intraperitoneal injections of LT1002 at doses of 30 or 90 mg/kg or vehicle once daily for 1 or 7 days. Blood samples collected on Days 1 and 7 showed no statistically significant changes in ACT compared to vehicle controls. Statistical analysis confirmed no adverse impact on blood clotting times at either dose or time point. These results support the safety profile of LT1002 regarding coagulation parameters in this murine model.', 'topics': [{'topic': 'Study Design and Conduct', 'summary': 'Eighteen male and female C57/BL6 mice were assigned to three groups receiving vehicle, 30 mg/kg, or 90 mg/kg LT1002 via intraperitoneal injection once daily for 1 or 7 days. Three mice per sex per group were sacrificed on Days 1 and 7 for blood collection and ACT measurement. The study was conducted as a non-GLP safety pharmacology assessment.'}, {'topic': 'Test Article and Rationale', 'summary': 'LT1002 is a murine monoclonal antibody targeting sphingosine 1-phosphate (S1P), a bioactive lipid involved in angiogenesis and tumor growth. The murine antibody was used to minimize anti-human antibody responses in mice and to evaluate effects on blood clotting as part of preclinical safety assessment supporting clinical development of the humanized LT1009 antibody.'}, {'topic': 'Activated Clotting Time (ACT) Measurement', 'summary': 'Blood was collected via cardiac puncture under isoflurane anesthesia and immediately analyzed for ACT using a Hemochron 800 unit. ACT values were recorded on Days 1 and 7 to assess any acute or cumulative effects of LT1002 on coagulation.'}, {'topic': 'Results and Statistical Analysis', 'summary': 'Mean ACT values for vehicle, 30 mg/kg, and 90 mg/kg groups on Day 1 were 64.83, 61.17, and 71.17 seconds respectively, and on Day 7 were 69.17, 77.40, and 72.33 seconds respectively. These findings suggest LT1002 does not adversely affect coagulation parameters, supporting its safety in preclinical development.'}]}
